title: Storing and using leftover paint
subtitle: Keeping opened tins usable, recombining part-tins, and disposing of paint that cannot be saved
excerpt: The average UK household has around 5 litres of usable leftover paint. Most of it sits unused in sheds for years, then goes to landfill. Proper sealing keeps water-based paint usable for 3 to 5 years; recombining same-type leftover tins creates a useful mixed colour. Community schemes accept usable paint and redistribute it.
sourceNotes: Community RePaint UK scheme guidance on paint donation standards. WRAP (Waste and Resources Action Programme) paint waste data: average UK household paint waste statistics. Paintback (Australia) guidance on paint storage and reconstitution (adapted for UK water-based/oil-based types). gov.uk guidance on WEEE and hazardous household waste disposal.

glossaryTerms.definition: Paints using water as the carrier, including emulsion, acrylic, and latex types. These are the most common household paints and are easier to dispose of safely than oil-based types.

content.text: keeps for 3 to 5 years if stored correctly: sealed against air, kept frost-free, and stored upright. Oil-based paints and varnishes last 2 to 3 years if sealed well. Most leftover paint goes to waste not because it has aged out but because it dries in a poorly sealed tin or freezes.
Wipe the lid recess clean of paint with a rag before closing. A dried ring of paint in the recess prevents the lid from sealing fully.
Press the lid down firmly around the full perimeter. Use a rubber mallet, not a hammer, to avoid denting the lid and distorting the seal.
For less than 500 ml remaining, transfer to a smaller container. A glass jar with a screw lid or a clean food tub works well. This reduces the air space above the paint.
Store upright in a frost-free location. Water-based paint freezes at 0°C and cannot be used after freeze-thaw cycling: the binders break down irreversibly.
Label the tin with the room it was used in and the date of last use.

A skin on water-based paint can be cut around the edge and removed. The paint beneath is usually still usable. Stir thoroughly with a stick or a drill-mounted paddle for 2 minutes. If it does not smooth out to a lump-free consistency after stirring, pass it through a fine mesh strainer (an old stocking works). If lumps persist after straining, the paint has degraded and should not be used.

Multiple part-tins of the same type (all water-based emulsion, or all oil-based gloss) can be combined in a bucket to create a larger quantity of a mixed colour. Do not combine water-based and oil-based paints. The result is useful for priming, undercoats, outdoor timber, and shed interior work where colour does not matter.

Community RePaint (communitypaint.org.uk) accepts usable paint with at least 1 litre remaining, a sealed tin, and no more than 5 years old. They redistribute it to community projects and households in need. Check the postcode finder on their website for the nearest scheme.
Disposing of paint that cannot be saved

Water-based paint can be dried and then placed in normal household waste (not recycling). Open the tin, leave in a ventilated place until solid. Dry sand or cat litter speeds the process for large volumes.
Oil-based paint, varnish, and solvent-based products are hazardous household waste. Take to your local household waste recycling centre (HWRC).

rows.symptom: Paint has a sour or rotten smell when the tin is opened
rows.cause: Bacterial contamination of water-based paint, common if water was left in the tin or the brush was not cleaned before dipping
rows.fix: Dispose of smelly paint; it cannot be saved. To prevent in future, always use a clean brush and do not add water to a partly used tin.
